summary: The environment and skills provide what a developer needs to start the sample: Python, Node, Docker, Azure CLI, the documentdb MCP server, and a rich set of DocumentDB agent skills. The inventory shows the live vector-capable Azure DocumentDB cluster is reachable (via the documentdb MCP profile) and the MCP tooling to inspect collections/indexes is available. Several cold-answer facts from the model were incorrect or described neighbouring services (Cosmos DB RU, older 'DocumentDB' name, or Amazon DocumentDB). Those confusions are documented below with authoritative grounding and concrete guidance the builder must apply. Missing accelerators (local DocumentDB container, optional agent toolkit CLI install) and some unspecified app choices (embedding model, LLM provider, response shape) leave the build able to proceed but with assumptions to record.
summary_points: The build can start now: required runtime and data-plane tools (python, pip, node, docker, az, and the documentdb MCP server) are available and connected to the live cluster.

Many model cold-answers confused Azure DocumentDB with Cosmos DB or other neighbours — especially resource type, CLI commands, connection host suffix/port, RU billing, vector-index syntax and text/vector search primitives.
Installed DocumentDB skills (vector-search, driver, connection, indexing, local-deploy, etc.) cover most implementation guidance; use them (load_skill) when writing code or index definitions.
Missing optional accelerators: a local DocumentDB container for offline testing and a documented agent-kit install step; these would speed development but are not blocking.

Key unknowns the builder must decide up-front: embedding model/dimension, which LLM provider and model, response API shape (include similarity scores?), and seed-data size/format — document these as assumptions in the README.

No single required tool is missing that blocks the sample, but several cold-answer corrections are essential: use az documentdb mongocluster commands and Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in IaC, use the DocumentDB vector index APIs (cosmosSearch / cosmosSearchOptions), and prefer vCore compute-tier billing (Mxx) for Azure DocumentDB.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: databaseAccounts (full resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for the managed MongoDB cluster is microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource type name 'mongoClusters').

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Azure used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for the earlier DocumentDB/Cosmos DB service; the new managed MongoDB offering uses a distinct resource type (mongoClusters). Shared 'DocumentDB' name and legacy Cosmos DB naming cause mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in IaC or CLI will target the wrong resource type (Cosmos DB accounts) and fail to create/modify the DocumentDB mongo cluster. Templates and ARM/Bicep must use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.
improvements: Update any agent kit documentation and code samples to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters where appropriate (Quickstart Bicep and Azure CLI examples).
Add a note in the agent skill describing the resource-type difference vs legacy Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts'.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --locations regionName=westus --capabilities EnableMongo. (az cosmosdb is a built-in core az command group, not an extension.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb command group and its subcommands for mongoClusters (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show). The 'documentdb' extension/command group (and az documentdb) is the supported CLI surface for Azure DocumentDB clusters.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: az cosmosdb historically targets Cosmos DB account management; the new DocumentDB (vCore) offering introduced 'az documentdb' and 'mongocluster' command group. Shared wording (cosmosdb / documentdb) caused the mistake.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster create (legacy/other CLI group)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands will manage Cosmos DB accounts and not the microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resources; deployment and CLI examples must call az documentdb mongocluster.*.
improvements: Document the correct az documentdb mongocluster commands in the sample README and any agent templates.
Add a short CLI snippet in the documentdb-mcp-setup skill that shows az documentdb mongocluster create/update/show.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (AzureRM provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" for Cosmos DB accounts (set the kind/api and capabilities for MongoDB compatibility).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type in Bicep/ARM (and corresponding AzAPI/Terraform definitions referencing Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters). The vCore 'mongoClusters' resource is the correct target (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform documentation)
Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB accounts (databaseAccounts) used to host MongoDB-compatible endpoints for the Cosmos DB RU model. The vCore offering uses a different resource type (mongoClusters) so older IaC examples mislead agents.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong resource type will create or change a Cosmos DB account rather than the intended vCore DocumentDB cluster, producing deployment failures or wrong resource arcs.
improvements: Add a short 'Which IaC resource to use' note to the documentdb-azure-deployment skill that clearly contrasts Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters vs Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
Provide a Bicep snippet for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in the sample README.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible connection strings for Cosmos DB: SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&w=majority Non-SRV: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false Notes: host suffix is "*.mongo.cosmos.azure.com" (or <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com), port 10255 for direct TLS connections, TLS/SSL (tls=true or ssl=true) must be enabled, replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false are commonly required options for Cosmos DB's Mongo-compatible endpoint.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB clusters use cluster-specific hostnames under the *.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) host suffix and the SRV scheme mongodb+srv is recommended. The cluster gateway uses port 10260 (and 10260.. for additional shards when 'query from any node' is enabled). TLS (tls=true/ssl=true) is required. Microsoft Entra ID (MONGODB-OIDC) or native authentication are supported depending on cluster auth config — do not assume the Cosmos DB host suffix or port 10255 used by older Cosmos DB Mongo endpoints.

grounding_links.title: Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the older Cosmos DB for MongoDB account hostnames (mongo.cosmos.azure.com) and port 10255; Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters) uses a different host pattern and port range (10260 etc). The shared 'Mongo-compatible' naming and past Cosmos usage caused the mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (legacy docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port (10255 and *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com) will fail to connect to the vCore cluster; using SRV with the cluster's mongocluster domain and enabling TLS is required. Authentication mechanism also differs: the cluster can accept MONGODB-OIDC when configured.
improvements: Update agent kit examples and the sample's .env.example to show the recommended SRV hostname pattern (mongodb+srv://<client>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and mention the 10260 gateway port and 'query from any node' port range.
Add a short note in documentdb-mcp-setup clarifying differences vs 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com' connection strings.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) is billed using Request Units (RUs) for throughput; you provision throughput at database or container level (manual RUs) or use autoscale. There are also serverless/account-level modes for some scenarios. (Note: some newer managed MongoDB offerings on Azure expose vCore-based SKUs, but the classic Cosmos DB/Mongo-compatible API is RU-based.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore-managed Mongo-compatible offering) is billed by compute (cluster tier, e.g., M30, M40 — vCores and RAM) and storage. It does not charge RUs; compute (per-tier) + storage are the billing model. This differs from Cosmos DB's RU-based model.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Compute and storage configurations for Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's RU model. Azure DocumentDB (vCore) intentionally uses vCore cluster tiers (Mxx). Shared historical names (DocumentDB, Cosmos) create confusion.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RU-based provisioning, they will attempt to set throughput and RU-related configuration (wrong resource model). The sample must choose compute tier M30 (or what's in run environment) and not try to provision RUs.
improvements: Add an explicit 'billing model' note to the sample README: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore) uses compute-tier (Mxx) + storage, not RUs'.
Add a short comparison page in the agent kit highlighting the difference between Azure DocumentDB (vCore) and Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU).

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary supported auth for the MongoDB-compatible endpoint is username/password (the MongoDB username and the account primary key or user password). Cosmos DB supports resource tokens and keys. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is supported for Cosmos DB's SQL/Core API, but direct MongoDB-protocol authentication via AAD is generally not supported — MongoDB drivers should use the user/password credentials in the connection string (TLS required).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (native users / SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication for data-plane access when enabled. The cluster can be configured to allow NativeAuth and MicrosoftEntraID modes and drivers can connect using MONGODB-OIDC (mongodb+srv with authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC) or use native SCRAM credentials depending on cluster auth settings.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (azure-portal)
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference) — auth modes

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflects older Cosmos DB Mongo endpoints where AAD auth was less common; the vCore DocumentDB offering added explicit Microsoft Entra ID support and OIDC flows for Mongo drivers. Shared 'Mongo-compatible' label hides this capability change.

confusion_sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only username/password, they might miss implementing OIDC flows for managed identities when the cluster is configured with MicrosoftEntraID; conversely, trying OIDC in clusters not configured for it will fail. The sample should read DOCUMENTDB_URI from env (native credentials) by default and document how to switch to Entra/OIDC if needed.
improvements: Add a 'how to authenticate' section to the sample README that shows both native SCRAM and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) examples with the connection-string examples and required connection options.
Add a snippet in documentdb-mcp-setup showing how to check a cluster's allowed auth modes.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Python use pymongo/MongoClient). Do not use the azure-cosmos SDK for MongoDB wire-protocol interactions; azure-cosmos is for the SQL/Core API. There is no separate MongoDB-protocol-specific Microsoft SDK — use upstream MongoDB drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python) for data-plane access over the MongoDB wire protocol. The azure-cosmos SDK targets the SQL/Core API and is not appropriate for DocumentDB (mongoClusters) protocol interactions.

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: Connect a Node.js web app with Azure DocumentDB
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: I expect Azure's DocumentDB (Mongo-compatible) vector indexes to follow a MongoDB-style knn/vector index syntax. Example (MongoDB 7-style hypothetical): db.high_risk_profiles.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } }) — alternatively a server command like db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'high_risk_profiles', indexes: [{ key: { embedding: 'knnVector' }, name: 'embedding_knn', knnVector: { dimensions:1536, method:'hnsw', ... } }] }) . (I am not certain of the exact option names; this is the concrete command I would try first.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports three integrated vector index algorithms: vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, and vector-diskann (names used in the cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions index definitions). You create them using createIndexes (with 'cosmosSearch' key and 'cosmosSearchOptions') or the createIndexes runCommand template that sets cosmosSearchOptions.kind to 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' and supplies algorithm-specific parameters (dimensions, m, efConstruction, numLists, maxDegree, lBuild, etc.). Searches use the $search stage with the cosmosSearch operator.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (IVF example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed MongoDB's upcoming knnVector index syntax; Azure DocumentDB exposes vector indexes via a cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions API and a different 'kind' naming convention (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder issues the wrong createIndex shape (knnVector), the server will reject it. Use the documented cosmosSearchOptions payload and the $search aggregation stage for vector queries.
improvements: Update any agent skill examples that attempt to create vector indexes to use the cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions shape and include example parameters (dimensions, similarity, m/efConstruction, numLists, lBuild).
Include a ready-made createIndexes JSON blob in the sample's seed script and a fallback that logs the exact server error when the index create fails.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: For simple text search, use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' }) and queries with $text) supported by the MongoDB driver. For hybrid vector+text search, you typically combine a vector KNN index on the embedding field with a text index or use an external service (Azure Cognitive Search) to perform hybrid ranking. If the service exposes a native vector+text search primitive, you would run a specialized aggregate/search stage (e.g., a $search/$searchMeta or knn stage) — otherwise implement a two-step approach: vector nearest-neighbour retrieval then text filtering/scoring.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides an integrated full-text search engine (BM25) exposed via createSearchIndexes and the $search operator, and an integrated vector engine exposed via createIndexes + cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions + $search (cosmosSearch operator). Hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector) is supported and documented: you run separate keyword ($search with text index) and vector ($search with cosmosSearch) queries and fuse results (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) either client-side or server-side (via $unionWith and grouping). You do NOT need an external Azure Cognitive Search for hybrid text+vector scenarios.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB
Hybrid search

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the common two-step approach used when a DB lacks integrated vector/text features; Azure DocumentDB integrates both engines and provides server-side fusion mechanisms, so an external search service is unnecessary for many hybrid scenarios.

confusion_sources.title: Full-text search and hybrid search docs

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses an external search service unnecessarily, the sample becomes more complex and slower and will duplicate index/ingest logic. Use the integrated search/index APIs for hybrid retrieval.
improvements: Add a short hybrid-search example to documentdb-vector-search and the sample README demonstrating server-side RRF fusion with $unionWith and the client-side fallback.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB-compatible API supports specific MongoDB wire protocol/feature versions depending on the account's configuration (historically 3.2, 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 4.4 and later added 5.0/6.0 support; newer accounts may advertise MongoDB 7.0 compatibility). Not all MongoDB server features are implemented — differences commonly include limited or different transaction semantics, differences in aggregation pipeline stage behavior, limited server-side JavaScript (no $where), and gaps in some admin/replica-set commands. Expect to use standard drivers but verify specific aggregation stages and admin operations against the target account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol/server versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (per current docs) and provides a high degree of operator coverage (~99.03%), but some administrative commands and PaaS-managed behaviours differ (platform manages replication, certain admin commands are not exposed, and a few aggregation variables/stages are omitted). The compatibility matrix in the documentation lists supported operators and commands per server-version compatibility.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (MongoDB compatibility)
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed Cosmos DB legacy compatibility statements with the new vCore DocumentDB compatibility claims; the latest docs enumerate support for wire protocol versions up to 8.0—more specific than the cold answer.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a lower or different server-version could lead to misusing features or mis-setting the serverVersion in provisioning. Check the cluster's serverVersion and test critical aggregation stages against the cluster.
improvements: Add a 'supported server versions' check in the documentdb-mcp-setup skill that returns the configured serverVersion for the cluster.
Reference the operator compatibility matrix when giving code samples that rely on specific aggregation stages.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is a Cosmos DB emulator for the SQL/Core API, but it does not emulate the MongoDB-protocol endpoint reliably. For local development targeting the MongoDB protocol, run a local MongoDB server (official Docker image) e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:7 and connect to mongodb://localhost:27017. If you must test Cosmos DB-specific behaviour, test against the real Azure account (no faithful local emulator for Mongo endpoint).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a local DocumentDB gateway Docker image for development and evaluation that listens on port 10260 by default (gateway endpoint). You can run ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest and connect on mongodb://localhost:10260 (TLS, usually --tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for local testing). The Cosmos DB emulator is not a suitable substitute for this DocumentDB local gateway; a plain local mongo:latest is not functionally equivalent if you want DocumentDB-specific behaviour.

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: Build a TypeScript app with DocumentDB and deploy to Azure DocumentDB (local gateway)
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer recommended a raw MongoDB container as a general substitute; the DocumentDB project provides a dedicated gateway image (port 10260) that better mirrors the managed service behaviour and features.
confusions.build_risk: Using a plain mongo:latest container can mask DocumentDB-specific behaviors (ports, TLS, index APIs, vector search) and lead to failing samples when run against the live cluster. For integration tests of DocumentDB features, use the DocumentDB local gateway image or test against the live cluster.
improvements: Add a local-dev subsection in documentdb-local-deployment skill showing the docker pull/run command and port 10260, and include an env var example connecting to the local gateway.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically change streams (the MongoDB change stream feature) were not fully supported on Cosmos DB's MongoDB API; instead Cosmos DB provides its own Change Feed for the SQL/Core API. If newer Mongo-compatible accounts advertise change stream support, you may need to target a compatible server-version API level; otherwise rely on Cosmos DB Change Feed or poll/maintain oplog-like mechanisms. In short: do not assume change streams work unless the account/platform explicitly documents support and you set the account to a compatible MongoDB wire version.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams, including multi-shard change streams (preview) and options such as pre-images and updateDescription when enabled. Some change-stream features for multishard/resumability require enabling the feature in the cluster (shown under Features in the portal or via CLI) and respecting the documented limitations. Change streams are supported for inserts/updates/deletes and are resumable with resume tokens.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Change streams — multi-shard preview and enabling

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected older limitations of Cosmos DB's Mongo API; the vCore DocumentDB offering exposes robust change stream support and configuration options.

confusion_sources.title: Change streams docs and enabling multi-shard

confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are unsupported would lead the builder to implement polling or other brittle workarounds. Conversely, using change streams without enabling required cluster features will fail. The sample should check cluster features and document how to enable change streams if the sample depends on them.
improvements: Add a check in documentdb-mcp-setup that queries whether change streams are enabled and instructs the builder how to enable them via az documentdb mongocluster update or the portal.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (service-specific MCP) for data-plane inspection and index/collection exploration; the general Azure MCP server covers broad resource management but may not include the service-specific data-plane helpers for DocumentDB/Mongo-compatible operations. For collection/index inspection and query plans use the documentdb profile/tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the dedicated 'documentdb' MCP server exposes data-plane tools (list databases, createIndex, aggregate, explain, insert_documents, list_indexes, etc.) for DocumentDB. The general azure MCP server is for control-plane/resource operations; use the documentdb MCP server to inspect collections, indexes and run aggregation/explain operations.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name/early service that Microsoft later rebranded and expanded as Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB now exposes multiple APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra-compatible, Gremlin, Table). This Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is distinct from any unrelated open-source projects with similar names; Azure's DocumentDB was Microsoft's proprietary service that evolved into Cosmos DB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly true but ambiguous: 'Azure DocumentDB' historically referred to the original DocumentDB service (which later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB). Separately, the vCore offering formerly named 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' has been renamed to 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' and is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (distinct from the original 2014-era DocumentDB). Also, Azure DocumentDB (vCore) and Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) are distinct services with different billing and resource models.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming/history)
Azure DocumentDB release notes (rename note)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The name 'DocumentDB' has been used at different times for different products (original DocumentDB → Cosmos DB; later vCore Mongo offering renamed to Azure DocumentDB). Shared names across product iterations cause ambiguity.

confusion_sources.title: FAQ: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB?

confusions.build_risk: Documentation or sample text that refers casually to 'Azure DocumentDB' without clarifying which incarnation (old Cosmos DocumentDB vs new vCore DocumentDB) will confuse users and cause wrong SDK/CLI choices.
improvements: Require explicit phrasing in samples and READMEs: e.g., 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore, MongoDB-compatible)' and add a short parenthetical: '(not the 2014–2017 Azure DocumentDB that became Cosmos DB)'.
Add a deprecation/rename note where older docs remain live to guide readers to the current product pages.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is Azure Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed storage/engine; the MongoDB compatibility layer implements the Mongo wire protocol on top of that engine. That means you use standard MongoDB drivers, but some server behaviors, query planner choices, and admin commands may differ — test queries and features against the target account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project, built on PostgreSQL internals for storage) and exposes the MongoDB wire protocol compatibility layer. This means application code uses standard MongoDB drivers but should test for implementation differences; however DocumentDB is not the Cosmos DB proprietary engine in this offering (it is based on the open-source DocumentDB engine).

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed a Cosmos DB proprietary engine under the Mongo compatibility; the current vCore offering is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine, which changes some portability and licensing assumptions.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the Cosmos engine might lead the builder to expect Cosmo-specific behaviors or to pick azure-cosmos SDK; instead they should use Mongo drivers and be aware of DocumentDB-specific behaviors documented in compatibility tables.
improvements: Clarify in agent skills and sample README that Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine and that standard MongoDB drivers are the supported client surface.

confusions.question: What connection mechanism and environment variable will the sample use to reach the cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the MongoDB-compatible connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it directly to pymongo.MongoClient, e.g. MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']). The connection string must include TLS (ssl=true/tls=true) and the account credentials.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct per the run-environment notes: the sample should read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to the MongoDB driver (pymongo.MongoClient). The connection string must include TLS and credentials or be an SRV URI; secrets must not be written to logs.
confusions.grounding_source: sample prompt run environment (skill_md) and quickstart docs

confusions.question: What database/collection names and embedding field will the sample create and use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name sample_healthcare_13. Create a collection named high_risk_profiles to store high-risk patient profiles; store embeddings in a field named embedding (an array of floats). Also create a collection named patient_sessions or agent_memory for agent conversation state and references.
confusions.grounded_answer: The run environment explicitly prescribes database sample_healthcare_13. Collection names and field names are not mandated by service docs, but using a single collection high_risk_profiles with an 'embedding' numeric[] field is consistent with DocumentDB vector index requirements; a separate collection for agent memory (agent_memory or patient_sessions) is reasonable but is a design choice left to the builder.
confusions.grounding_source: sample prompt run environment (skill_md) and vector-index docs

grounding_links.title: Run environment (sample prompt)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (requirements for vector field)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Database name was provided in the run-environment; collection/schema names were not mandated and the cold answer made a reasonable choice. This is not an API-level fact error but a design choice that the builder must confirm.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder names the collection differently than what their verification scripts expect, automated checks will fail. Document chosen collection/field names in README and seed scripts.
improvements: Add a convention note in the sample README declaring the collection and field names (e.g., high_risk_profiles.embedding) and ensure the seed script uses them.

confusions.question: What index definition will the sample attempt to create for vector search (concrete command to try)?
confusions.cold_answer: Try to create a knn vector index on the embedding field with a createIndexes command. Example (run via pymongo db.command): db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'high_risk_profiles', indexes: [{ key: { embedding: 'knnVector' }, name: 'embedding_knn', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } }] }) — adjust dimensions and method if the server rejects the option names. If the server requires a different API, fall back to storing embeddings and using an approximate nearest neighbour retrieval client-side.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the Azure DocumentDB vector-index syntax: runCommand createIndexes with key: { '<path>': 'cosmosSearch' } and cosmosSearchOptions specifying kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann', dimensions, similarity and algorithm-specific params (m/efConstruction, numLists, lBuild, etc.). Example JSON is documented and the sample should parameterize dimensions to match the embedding model used.

Perform vector similarity search (cosmosSearch operator)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer tried to apply MongoDB 7.0 knnVector syntax; Azure DocumentDB uses a cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions index definition instead.

confusion_sources.title: Quickstart: Vector index with .NET in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: Issuing the incorrect createIndexes payload will cause index creation to fail; ensure the seed script uses the documented cosmosSearchOptions shape and verifies the created index with list_indexes or the MCP 'documentdb_list_indexes' tool.
improvements: Include a tested createIndexes payload in the sample's seed script and an explain or list_indices verification step using the documentdb MCP tools.

confusions.question: Which client libraries and runtime will the sample use to implement LlamaIndex + Mongo storage and retrieval?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Python with pymongo (MongoClient) for database access, LlamaIndex for the agent/LLM orchestration, and a standard embedding model (e.g., OpenAI/other) to convert clinical features into embeddings. Implement a retriever that queries the DocumentDB vector index (via the server-side knn index if available) using pymongo aggregate/runCommand; otherwise implement a client-side ANN fallback using faiss or hnswlib for nearest-neighbour retrieval and store IDs in Mongo.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is a valid and practical stack: Python + pymongo for data-plane access, LlamaIndex for agent orchestration, and an embedding model (OpenAI or other) for transforms. For vector retrieval prefer server-side cosmosSearch / $search (cosmosSearch operator) when DocumentDB indexes exist; fallback to a client-side ANN (faiss/hnswlib) only if server-side vector indexes are unavailable. The builder must choose the embedding model/dimensions and ensure the vector index dimensions match.

confusions.question: How will the application authenticate to the cluster in this sample run environment?
confusions.cold_answer: Authenticate using the MongoDB connection string (username/password) contained in DOCUMENTDB_URI. The username is the configured Mongo user and the password is the account primary key or the user password created for the Mongo endpoint; TLS must be used. Do not attempt Azure AD authentication for the Mongo driver in this sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: By default and per the sample run-environment, the builder should use the connection string in DOCUMENTDB_URI (native credentials with TLS). The cluster also supports Microsoft Entra ID OIDC authentication when configured; the sample should document both options and default to DOCUMENTDB_URI for reproducible runs. Do not write secrets to logs.
confusions.grounding_source: sample prompt run environment and auth docs

grounding_links.title: Run environment (sample prompt)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer recommended only native credentials; while native credentials are the default for the sample, the service also supports Entra/OIDC when configured — the sample should document both methods and choose native SCRAM as default for reproducibility.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts OIDC without cluster-side configuration, connections will fail. The sample should default to DOCUMENTDB_URI (native) and include a note about OIDC/Entra option.
improvements: Add a small 'auth options' section to .env.example that documents DOCUMENTDB_URI (native) and how to switch to Entra/OIDC if the cluster supports it.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and dimensionality
information_gaps.description: The prompt and skills do not specify which embedding model (provider/model name) to use or the embedding vector dimension (e.g., text-embedding-3-small = 1536). The builder must pick a model and set the vector index dimensions accordingly. I searched Microsoft docs and the run-environment but found no mandated model.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and chat model for LlamaIndex agent
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt requests a LlamaIndex agent but does not name the LLM/chat provider or model to use for reasoning/narrative generation. The builder must decide (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, local model) and document how to configure API keys. I looked through the prompt, skills and Learn docs; none prescribe a default.

information_gaps.title: Response schema and similarity scores
information_gaps.description: It is not specified whether the sample's API should return retrieved profile documents and numeric similarity scores alongside the generated narrative. This affects the query projection and $project use ($meta: 'searchScore') as well as README/CLI output. Not answered by docs or the run-environment text.

information_gaps.title: Seed data format and idempotency
information_gaps.description: No canonical sample dataset or required seed size is provided. The builder must create a synthetic-data generator and ensure the seed script is idempotent (upsert by patient_id). No skill or doc prescribes a sample dataset or seeding strategy.

information_gaps.title: LlamaIndex integration pattern for DocumentDB retriever
information_gaps.description: There is no out-of-the-box LlamaIndex connector for Azure DocumentDB in the installed skills. The builder must implement a retriever that calls pymongo aggregates with $search/cosmosSearch or wraps the DocumentDB vector API. The agent toolkit doesn't include a turnkey LlamaIndex->DocumentDB retriever mapping.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type and az documentdb mongocluster commands (not az cosmosdb or databaseAccounts) when referring to the DocumentDB vCore cluster in CLI, Bicep, Terraform or deployment scripts.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: azd (Azure Developer CLI) is not required for this sample. If you want to add CI/CD or quick 'azd' templates, install azd via package manager (see Azure docs). Not necessary for building the Python LlamaIndex sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is not required to run the sample (a pre-provisioned cluster is provided). If you want to include IaC artifacts for the cluster, install the 'bicep' CLI (learn.microsoft.com Bicep install). For the sample, document that Bicep/Terraform templates exist and where to find them.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform is optional. If the project will include Terraform-based deployment artifacts for reproducible infra, add Terraform to PATH. Otherwise, skip; the sample uses an existing cluster.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: dotnet is not required for this Python sample; only add if you intend to build .NET quickstarts or run .NET-based verification scripts.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: mongosh is useful for manual verification and debugging (connect to SRV cluster and test queries). Install mongosh to allow human-in-the-loop checks and to run quick manual $search queries if needed.
